A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research framework, renamed from SecFwT to SecP-Tuning. All 17 pages of each version, including figures, tables, equations and appendices, are available and readable.

before.justification: V1 reports original RoBERTaLARGE task performance, attention-efficiency measurements, and LAN/WAN and serviceability experiments in Figures 1 and 3 and Tables 1–4.

after.justification: V2 reports original RoBERTaLARGE performance and efficiency experiments, including gradient-based prompt-tuning comparisons, in Figures 1 and 3 and Tables 1–4.

M1.justification: The framework retains client-side loss evaluation and CMA-ES prompt optimization, secret-shared server inference, and the same RFA and cosine protocols. The expanded seven-step overview and newly documented initialization and hyperparameters do not establish a changed method.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate SST-2, Yelp Polarity, AG’s News, MRPC and RTE, with the same LAN/WAN scenarios and attention-length coverage. V2 replaces the loose GLUE description with explicit dataset names. Its MNLI example concerns pretrained prompt initialization and does not establish an additional evaluated task.

E2.justification: V2 replaces Full+RFA with gradient-based Prompt Tuning in the task-performance and LAN/WAN comparisons, and adds Prompt Tuning to the deployment comparison. Full+SM and FoT+SM remain under the names SFT and SecP-Tuning (FoT), respectively.

E3.justification: The new prompt-tuning comparison introduces Adam training at learning rate 5e-4 for 1000 epochs with matched prompt initialization, templates and label words. V2 also adds accuracy to the deployment evaluation and communication profiling across three sequence lengths in Figure 1. Newly disclosed settings for retained experiments do not establish that their earlier protocols changed.

E4.justification: Figure 1 adds analysis of how backward/optimizer and softmax communication costs scale with sequence length. Removing Full+RFA eliminates the earlier check of RFA under full tuning, although FoT versus FoT+RFA remains. Figure 3’s attention-length analysis and the SST-2/AG’s News deployment case study already existed despite their placement under the new Ablation Studies heading.

E5.justification: Both task-performance tables report means and standard deviations over three runs, and both LAN/WAN timing tables report averages over ten runs. V2 introduces no new experimental seed identities, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The five-task tables reverse the proposed method’s average ranking against full tuning: 75.70 versus 79.88 in v1 becomes 82.45 versus 79.90 in v2. WAN timings, deployment costs and Figure 1 findings are extensively revised, with new prompt-tuning and deployment-accuracy entries. The proposed method’s LAN total remains 55.172 seconds; its larger reported speedup follows revised baseline timings. These are changed reported outcomes, without established equivalence of all underlying settings across versions.

T1.justification: The RFA derivation, prompt-subspace objective, Algorithms 1–2, underlying MPC formulas and composable-security argument are retained. Equation renumbering, equivalent notation and the dedicated threat-model subsection introduce no substantive mathematical or proof changes.

C1.justification: V1 emphasizes efficient general LLM fine-tuning with comparable or slightly degraded performance. V2 narrows the stated contribution to prompt tuning and claims superior average performance against SFT and gradient-based prompt tuning. API deployability and avoidance of parameter-transmission leakage become central parts of its claimed combined advantage.

C2.justification: V2 replaces the discussion of multiclass performance loss and additional optimization iterations with a hypothesis that CMA-ES exploration avoids small-data overfitting. It adds explanations for prompt-tuning overhead, amplified WAN advantages and comparative privacy benefits. V1’s explicit architecture and nonlinear-operation limitations are removed, while v2 adds a qualification about choosing semi-honest security over malicious security for efficiency.

D1.justification: V2 adds Appendix 6.5 and substantial implementation information, including 50 prompt tokens, a 500-dimensional search subspace, 128 random features, an 8000-call budget, pretrained prompt initialization and early-stopping patience of 1000. Baseline optimizer settings and training budgets are also specified. Conversely, v1’s paper-specific code-availability statement and link disappear; the CrypTen link remains.

R1.justification: The related-work discussion substantially repositions the framework against HE-based adaptation, adding BlindTuner, MedBlindTuner and FedShield-LLM and expanding the MPC-versus-HE comparison. PrivTuner’s characterization changes, and the Lee et al. classification-head discussion is removed. Rho et al. 2025 matches the earlier 2024 reference rather than constituting a new work.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method motivation and experimental narrative are extensively rewritten. Related work and preliminaries become separate sections, the threat model receives its own subsection, and the appendices lose Limitations and gain Hyperparameters. The title, method name and author/affiliation presentation also change.

P2.justification: Figure 1 replaces two nested breakdown charts with four panels, including sequence-length bar charts. Figure 2 is redrawn with concrete prompt examples and revised flow labels. Performance and deployment tables exchange numbering and placement, several tables receive new structures and highlighting, and Table 5 is added. Figure 3 retains its existing plots.

improvement.justification: V2 improves assessability through the relevant prompt-tuning baseline, more precise scope and substantial hyperparameter disclosure. However, it removes explicit limitations and the paper-specific code link while strengthening comparative privacy claims without additional security evidence. Its revised SFT row also introduces a material inconsistency: Table 1’s timing components sum to 791.598 seconds, but the total is 651.598 seconds, weakening the headline speedup evidence. These benefits and harms leave the net quality direction uncertain.
